schools.summary: Gill reads the verb as a pluperfect, places Shittim in the plains of Moab and rejects the tradition that the spies were Caleb and Phinehas; Calvin distinguishes this errand from the twelve's survey and asks whether Joshua's prudence is to be approved or condemned as anxiety that did not consult God.
Henry recalls that Joshua had been one of the twelve and that it ended ill, and makes the case a rule: faith in the promise should encourage diligence, not supersede it.

Wesley reads the secrecy as directed at Israel rather than the enemy, lest a discouraging report get abroad; Clarke finds the king's summons revealing, since a guest under a householder's roof was sacred and had to be demanded rather than seized.
Keil and Delitzsch carry the report to its consequence, the king suspecting their errand and sending to Rahab to give them up.

debates.question: Was Joshua's sending of spies prudence or distrust?
debates.positions: Henry and Wesley take it for prudence that does not slacken faith; Calvin raises the possibility that Joshua trusted his own foresight without consulting God, and leaves the question open.

themes: faith that does not slacken diligence

schools.summary: Calvin dates the season from the drying flax and frames two questions he refuses to hurry, whether treachery to her country was excusable and whether the lie could be free from fault; Gill reads the verb as a pluperfect.

Clarke allows the darkness helped the plot but will excuse no prevarication, since God could have saved the messengers without her falsity and never says, Do evil that good may come; Wesley counts the hiding a generous act of faith while calling the answer unquestionably sinful.
Ellicott notes that flax and barley are early crops, and distinguishes the unvarying divine standard from the varying standard of a believer's conscience.

debates.question: Was Rahab’s falsehood sinful, and if so how is she praised for the act it served?
debates.positions: Clarke and Wesley call the lie sinful outright, Wesley allowing that a heathen might think an officious lie no crime; Ellicott says it left no stain on her conscience though all falsehood is sin; Calvin raises the question of treachery to her country alongside it and settles neither quickly.

outliers.view: That the divine standard of sin never varies while the standard of a believer's conscience may vary considerably, so that the falsehood was sin and yet left her conscience unstained.

themes: stalks of flax on the roof
the season fixed by the crop
the gate shut behind the pursuers

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark the pronouns, the terror having fallen on the Canaanites at large rather than Jericho only, and hear in her words the song sung at the sea now reported as accomplished fact; they judge her confession short of what Moses was demanding of Israel.
Henry makes the speech the whole justification of the mission, the deliverance from Egypt being remembered afresh in Jericho forty years after.

Calvin weighs the two reports as proofs of unequal force, the opened sea irrefragable and the victories inferential, and reads her confession as faith seen in a mirror though still only a germ of piety; Gill fastens on the forty-year interval.
Clarke calls the confession amazingly full and offers three accounts of how she came by such knowledge without choosing between them; Wesley glosses the melting heart as courage dissolved.

debates.question: How did a Canaanite woman come by so full a confession of God?
debates.positions: Clarke offers three possibilities and decides among none of them, that some knowledge of the true God was general though tangled with local deities, that she had it from the spies in conversation, or that it came by supernatural influence on her soul.

debates.question: How developed was her faith at this point?
debates.positions: Calvin calls it a germ of piety, as yet insufficient of itself, while still proof of her election; Keil and Delitzsch judge it to fall short of what Moses then demanded of Israel.

themes: a song now reported as fact
God in heaven above and earth beneath

schools.summary: Calvin finds the deepest evidence of faith in what she assumes before asking, that the land is already given, and hears in it the apostle's sight of things that do not appear; Gill notes the Targum's form of the oath and reports Abarbinel on the absent husband and children.
Keil and Delitzsch define the true token as a sign of truth that proved to consist in nothing but the oath itself; Ellicott observes that she was in no way separated from her kindred.

Clarke takes the oath by the divine name as proof of instruction and glosses the pledge as the old practice of staking one life for another; Wesley notes that she asks nothing for herself and that the sequel far outran the request.

outliers.view: That Rahab was morally not inferior to her countrymen but rather their superior, publicans and harlots not being the worst members of the generation to whom the Word came.

themes: swear unto me by the LORD
our soul shall die for you
more than she could ask or think

schools.summary: Clarke explains the house on the wall and notes that the verse stands out of its place, since the descent cannot have preceded the terms agreed after it; Wesley reads the conversation as having passed indoors and reckons the three days as one whole day and parts of two.

Ellicott thinks the spies may have chosen the house because it let them leave without the gate, and denies that the scarlet line is the lowering cord, the words being different in the original; Keil and Delitzsch count three conditions and take the cord to be the rope of the previous verse.
Gill pictures the descent, recalls Paul let down the wall of Damascus, and identifies the mountain as the one now called Quarantania.

debates.question: Is the scarlet line in the window the same cord by which the spies were let down?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch take it for the rope of the previous verse, no other object having been named for the demonstrative, and Luther concluded the same; Wesley thinks it probably the same; Ellicott denies it flatly, the two being different words in the original, and it being preposterous to hang out the means of escape; Clarke calls it simply a piece of scarlet cloth used as a flag.

outliers.view: That the scarlet line belonged with the flax already on the roof, so that what hung at the window looked unremarkable while identifying the house to those in the secret.

themes: her house upon the town wall

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch give the second condition in its standing legal form, the blood upon a man's own head, and are careful that the binding of the cord is mentioned out of its time to close the subject; Ellicott sets the arrangement beside the charge given in Egypt.
Wesley paraphrases the two heads of blame and thinks she bound the line forthwith; Clarke judges the condition of secrecy prudently framed, her own life being staked upon it.
Gill sees the mischief guarded against, that others might hang out scarlet threads of their own or crowd into her house for shelter.

debates.question: When did Rahab bind the scarlet line in the window?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch hold she cannot have tied it at once but only when it was needed, the writer mentioning it early to close the subject; Wesley thinks she did it forthwith, so the spies might see it before departing and lest an accident occasion a neglect.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe the Quarantana range, a wall of rock twelve to fifteen hundred feet high full of caves and the nearest high ground to the city; Ellicott reads the three days by the usual inclusive reckoning.
Henry makes the safe return itself a token for good, since these spies had material enough to discourage and were of another spirit.

Clarke counts out the three days, contrasts the report with the earlier one, and returns at the close to the lie, allowing that she lied and holding that she was rewarded for hospitality and faith rather than falsehood; Wesley notes the provisions Rahab furnished and where the search went.
Calvin reads the report as a testimonial to the men's integrity and to God's indulgence in confirming the promise by experience; Gill reports Kimchi's reckoning of the day of descent.

outliers.view: That the inspired writer records Rahab's lie as a fact without making the Spirit of God responsible for it, and that she was rewarded for her hospitality and faith and not for the falsehood.

themes: a report the reverse of the first
rewarded for faith, not for falsehood
